## From counting to predicting

- Scalability was an important factor: ten billion *possible* cells at 100,000 words; batch PPMI–SVD counts first and factorizes afterwards
- word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013): learns vectors from local training pairs without building the matrix explicitly
- In skip-gram, a shallow network: the centre word's one-hot → that row of $\mathbf{W}$ (a lookup, no activation) → $\mathbf{W}'$ scores candidate contexts. In CBOW the context vectors are combined first
- Mostly $\mathbf{W}$ is kept; not a requirement

::: {.takeaway}
[We set up the prediction task to learn vectors we can reuse.]{.hl} A transformer's input embedding table (Chapter 7) works similarly; its rows belong to tokens.
:::

::: {.notes}
Counting works: royalty landed on one side and food on the other. Scalability was
an important factor in how quickly prediction-based methods were taken up; it is
not a distinction that holds for every count-based method.

Definition of word2vec: a family of methods from 2013 that learn word vectors from
context. Skip-gram predicts the context words from the centre word, and CBOW
predicts the centre word from the context words.

Three layers in skip-gram. The input layer is the centre word's one-hot vector.
The hidden layer multiplies it by W; multiplying a one-hot by a matrix selects that
word's row. So the hidden layer is a lookup table, often called a projection
layer. No further activation is applied. The output layer scores the selected
vector against candidate context words; for that we use a second table, W′, which
holds one row per word under the full softmax and under negative sampling alike.

Two matrices are learned: v for words as centres, u for words as contexts. In
classic word2vec use it is mostly v that is kept — a common choice, not a
requirement. Some approaches use the output matrix, or the sum or average of the
two; GloVe's authors recommend adding them (Pennington et al. 2014).
:::

## CBOW and skip-gram: arrows reversed

::: {.lede}
One window on *the pump failed during the night shift*: centre `failed`, width 2.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### CBOW · context → centre

[the]{.chip} [pump]{.chip} [during]{.chip} [the]{.chip} → average → `failed`

- One training example per window
- Usually faster; combines the context vectors
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Skip-gram · centre → context

`failed` → its own vector → [the]{.chip} [pump]{.chip} [during]{.chip} [the]{.chip}

- Four training examples per window
- More training pairs; can help on rare words
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
Both learn $\mathbf{W}$ (word → vector) and $\mathbf{W}'$ (scores partners); the pretrained vectors you download are mostly rows of $\mathbf{W}$. The rest of the chapter follows skip-gram, which is also what negative sampling is most often paired with.
:::

::: {.notes}
A static copy of the chapter's two-architecture figure. CBOW combines the vectors
of the surrounding words and predicts the centre. Skip-gram takes the centre word
and predicts each surrounding word in turn. (CBOW is the default in the original
word2vec tool and in `gensim`.)

Skip-gram pairs for the centre `failed`: (failed, the), (failed, pump),
(failed, during), (failed, the). In the book's interactive version students type a
sentence and move the centre and the window.

No hand annotation is needed; in the next step we give training labels to the
positive pairs and to sampled negative ones. Six billion tokens with a window of
five on each side produce at most 60 billion pairs; sentence boundaries,
subsampling and dynamic windows reduce that number.
:::

## Negative sampling with a logistic loss {.smaller}

- The full softmax computes and normalizes $V$ context scores for every training pair: about $O(Vd)$. Negative sampling changes the objective; the scoring cost is about $O((K+1)d)$
- The new question: [did this training example come from the observed pairs ($y=1$) or from the noise sampler ($y=0$)?]{.hl} The same pair can be produced either way. For each observed pair, $K$ contexts are drawn from a noise distribution $q$

$$P(y = 1 \mid w, c;\, K, q) = \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c), \qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$$

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c) - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \sigma(-\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_{n_k})$$

- The positive pair's term falls as the dot product grows; a negative sample's term falls as its dot product shrinks
- $K = 5$, $V = 400{,}000$: six dot products per pair in place of 400,000 — about 67,000 times fewer; the actual speed-up depends on hardware and implementation

::: {.src}
Mikolov et al. 2013
:::

::: {.notes}
Definition of negative sampling: for each observed word–context pair, drawing a
small number of contexts from a noise distribution and using them as negatively
labelled training examples. The negatives need not be unseen in the corpus or
semantically unrelated.

What the probability means: it belongs to the training sampling scheme we set up;
it is not the probability that two words occur together in the real world.

The pull-together, push-apart picture describes the change in score; it does not
say that the Euclidean distance between the vectors necessarily moves the same way.

The relation to logistic regression, in careful form: the sigmoid and the log loss
that SGNS uses for each labelled pair are familiar from logistic regression. But
the vectors on both sides of the dot product are learned too, so the model as a
whole is not classical logistic regression with fixed features. A more accurate
description is logistic matrix factorization, in which two vector tables are
learned together. That explains both the familiar form of the gradients and the
non-convexity of the joint optimization.

The chapter's figure: the left panel scores all 400,000 candidates and applies a
softmax; the right panel computes six dot products, for one positive (`pump`) and
five negatives (`opera`, `zinc`, `tariff`, `carbon`, `helix`).

The loss widget in the book: what is optimized directly is the word–context score,
not word–word similarity. Two words seen with similar contexts receive similar
updates and so move closer together.
:::

## Work one update by hand

::: {.lede}
Four dimensions in place of 300. Centre `failed`: $\mathbf{v} = (0.4,\ -0.2,\ 0.7,\ 0.1)$. Positive context `pump`: $\mathbf{u} = (0.5,\ 0.1,\ 0.6,\ -0.3)$. Sampled negative `opera`: $\mathbf{u} = (-0.3,\ 0.6,\ -0.2,\ 0.4)$.
:::

::: {.roomy}
| pair             | $y$ | $\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}$ | $\sigma(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u})$ | loss | $\sigma - y$ |
|:-----------------|----:|------------------------------:|--------------------------------------:|------:|-------------:|
| `failed`–`pump`  | 1   | 0.57                          | 0.639                                 | 0.448 | −0.361       |
| `failed`–`opera` | 0   | −0.34                         | 0.416                                 | 0.538 | 0.416        |
:::

- The derivative of one labelled term with respect to the dot product is $\sigma(z) - y$: [prediction minus target]{.hl}
- Update only $\mathbf{v}$ at learning rate 0.05: `failed`·`pump` 0.570 → **0.590**; `failed`·`opera` −0.340 → −0.359
- Update the context vectors too: 0.603 and −0.374 — the same directions, roughly 1.7 times as far

::: {.notes}
For the positive pair: (0.4)(0.5) + (−0.2)(0.1) + (0.7)(0.6) + (0.1)(−0.3) = 0.57.
So σ(0.57) = 0.639: under this training scheme the model gives the pair about a 64%
probability of having arrived as a positive example. Its contribution to the loss
is −log 0.639 = 0.448.

The negative pair's dot product is −0.34; its term uses σ(−z), so σ(0.34) = 0.584
and the loss is −log 0.584 = 0.538.

For `pump`, 0.639 − 1 = −0.361: negative, so the dot product goes up. For `opera`,
0.416 − 0 = 0.416: positive, so the dot product goes down.

With the context vectors fixed, the gradient of v is the sum of both terms:
(0.639 − 1)·u_pump + (0.416 − 0)·u_opera = (−0.305, 0.213, −0.300, 0.275). `gv` in
the training code computes it in one einsum.

The mathematics of one update is simple; quality is decided largely by which pairs
are shown, how often and against what — negative sampling, subsampling, the noise
distribution and the context window. Two slides on.
:::

## One pair touches at most seven rows

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{v}_w} = \bigl(\sigma(z) - y\bigr)\,\mathbf{u}_c, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{u}_c} = \bigl(\sigma(z) - y\bigr)\,\mathbf{v}_w$$

- The gradient of each vector is the scalar error $\sigma(z) - y$ times the other vector. When the correct label gets a high probability the scalar error is small; that alone does not guarantee stable training
- One pair with $K = 5$: one row of $\mathbf{W}$ and $1 + K$ rows of $\mathbf{W}'$ — **at most seven distinct rows**
- The remaining rows do not enter this pair's data loss; their gradients are [zero]{.hl}. Under SGD with no momentum and no weight decay those rows do not change
- The model we train from scratch has 37,354 rows; seven is about **0.019%**. A full softmax affects 18,678 rows, 2,668 times as many — a ratio of rows, not of running time

::: {.notes}
For those who want the derivation. Write z = v·u. σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)). By the
chain rule the derivative of −log σ(z) is σ(z) − 1. For a negative sample the term
is −log σ(−z) and the same two lines give σ(z). Both collapse into σ(z) − y.

The probabilistic reading: the label of every training example is 0 or 1, modelled
with a Bernoulli distribution. Its parameter p lies in [0, 1]; for finite z the
sigmoid produces p = σ(z) in (0, 1). −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)] is binary
cross-entropy, the negative log-likelihood of the Bernoulli model. Probability
estimates can also be evaluated with a squared loss; that is a different criterion.

Stability: vector norms can grow and the contributions within a batch can add up.
The learning rate, the gradient scale and, where needed, clipping have to be
considered separately.

The count: two tables of 18,677 words and 100 dimensions hold 37,354 rows and
3,735,400 parameters. If the sampled negatives repeat, or collide with the positive
context, fewer than seven distinct rows are touched. That sparsity is one of the
important reasons training is efficient.

Practical consequence: in SGNS the table is accessed only through the selected
indices, so the gradient of the data loss is sparse at the level of rows. PyTorch's
`nn.Embedding(..., sparse=True)` produces sparse gradients for accesses of this
kind. If the embedding parameters are also used in other operations, such as a
full softmax, the gradient of the whole parameter need not be sparse.
:::

## Four training choices that decide how well word2vec works {.smaller}

| choice | what it sets | typical value | effect |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Number of negatives** ($K$) | negatives per positive pair | 5–20 for a small corpus, 2–5 for a large one in the original work | changes the balance between cost and training signal |
| **Context window** | candidate neighbours and weighting by distance | for example at most 5, with a dynamic window | narrow windows can bring out functional relations more, wide ones topical relations |
| **Subsampling** ($t$) | probability of keeping very frequent tokens | for example $t = 10^{-3}$ | reduces the share of frequent words in training |
| **Noise distribution** | probability of drawing each negative | $q(w) \propto f(w)^{0.75}$ | raises the relative sampling share of rare words |

::: {.takeaway}
The update itself is simple. [What decides quality: which pairs you show, how often, and against what.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Number of negatives: with a very small K the model sees too few negative examples;
a large K makes every step more expensive. The original paper suggests 5–20 for
small corpora and 2–5 for large ones (Mikolov et al. 2013).

The context window: with a window of 5, up to five tokens to the left and right of
the centre, within the same input sequence, are candidate contexts. Narrow windows
(1–2) mostly reflect close syntactic relations and wide windows (5–10) topical
relations more. Those are tendencies; the corpus, the language and the
preprocessing affect the outcome too. If sentence boundaries are kept the window
does not cross them. word2vec does not keep the window fixed either: for each
centre it draws the effective width at random between 1 and the maximum, so near
neighbours produce pairs more often. Exercise 1 checks this by hand on the counting
method.

Subsampling and the noise distribution, with numbers, on the next slide.
:::

## Two of the choices, in numbers: subsampling and the 0.75 exponent

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
### Subsampling

| share of corpus  | example        | kept | discarded |
|:-----------------|:---------------|--------:|-------:|
| 5%               | `the`          | 0.16    | 84%    |
| 1%               | `of`, `and`    | 0.42    | 58%    |
| 0.1% ($= t$)     | mid-frequency  | 1.00    | 0%     |
| 0.01% and below  | the tail       | 1.00    | 0%     |

In our run 26.6% of the in-vocabulary tokens go: 6,397,826 → 4,698,743.
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .compact}
### Negatives are drawn with $f(w)^{0.75}$

- A word 5,000 times more frequent is only about 595 times more likely to be drawn — the gap narrows about eightfold
- The exponent raises the *relative* share of rare contexts; it adds no new kind of signal
- An empirical choice, not a theoretical optimum
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
Levy et al. (2015): hyperparameters of this kind [can affect comparison results substantially]{.hl}.
:::

::: {.notes}
Subsampling. Frequent words produce a large number of training pairs; to reduce
their relative influence each token is kept with a probability that depends on its
frequency: min(1, (sqrt(f/t) + 1) · t/f). Here f is the relative frequency among
the tokens left after the vocabulary filter, and t a threshold on the same scale.

Paper and code. The original C implementation uses that keep formula. The paper
gives P(discard) = 1 − sqrt(t/f); that expression is negative when f < t, so as a
probability it is read as max(0, 1 − sqrt(t/f)). The two formulas are not the same;
when reproducing an experiment, state which implementation was used.

Almost all of what the run discards is `the`, `of`, `and` and similar words.
(6,397,826 is what is left of the 6,794,527 tokens read once everything below
`min_count=20` is dropped.)

When a token is removed, the words on either side move closer together in the
remaining sequence. The window size does not change, but words that were further
apart in the original text can form new context pairs. That changes both the
number of examples and the context distribution.

The exponent. Raising probabilities to a power below 1 enlarges the smallest ones
most in relative terms: 0.5^0.75 is 19% larger than 0.5, and 0.001^0.75 is 5.6
times 0.001. 5000^0.75 ≈ 595. Negative samples make the context vectors receive
updates from pairs drawn from the noise distribution as well as from observed
positive pairs; the centre vectors are affected indirectly.
:::

## Writing it from scratch

::: {.lede}
NumPy, no framework; trained on the first 40 million characters of `text8`. The update step:
:::

```python
v = Wc[c]                                              # (B, D)
u = Wo[targets]                                        # (B, K+1, D)
score = sigmoid(np.einsum("bkd,bd->bk", u, v))         # (B, K+1)
err = (score - labels).astype(np.float32)              # predicted − observed
gv = np.einsum("bk,bkd->bd", err, u)
gu = err[:, :, None] * v[:, None, :]
np.clip(gv, -1.0, 1.0, out=gv)
np.clip(gu, -1.0, 1.0, out=gu)
np.add.at(Wc, c, -lr * gv)
np.add.at(Wo, targets.ravel(), (-lr * gu).reshape(-1, D))
```

::: {.takeaway}
`err = score - labels` is [predicted minus observed]{.hl}; every gradient is that difference times the other vector. After three epochs: `monday` → friday 0.87, `france` → spain 0.79, `physics` → mechanics 0.82.
:::

::: {.notes}
The full code is in the chapter and the notebook: a vocabulary with `min_count` 20
(18,677 words), subsampling, the 0.75 noise distribution, D = 100, K = 5, window 5,
3 epochs, learning rate 0.02, batches of 2,048. The basic gradient comes from the
logistic loss; the gradient clipping changes the update rule.

`sigmoid` is written in an overflow-safe form: np.exp(-np.logaddexp(0.0, -x)). It
does not artificially restrict the score to an interval.

The run: 6,794,527 tokens read; 4,698,743 after subsampling; 46,987,400 training
pairs; loss 4.159 → 2.350 (the loss at the end of an epoch is the mean of its last
1,000 batches); trained in 611 s. Other neighbours: `king` → consort 0.75, kings
0.75. `three` → four 0.95. `car` → racing 0.74, cars 0.74.

Two simplifications stated in the code: the window is fixed at 5, with no dynamic
window; and text8 is processed as a single token stream — the original sentence
and document boundaries are not kept, so artificial context pairs can form across
them. Batches are drawn with replacement; "3 epochs" here cannot be compared with
epochs = 3 in gensim.

The chapter's intuition check: why does `np.add.at` need gradient clipping here?
Batching accumulates every gradient of a repeated index and applies the sum in one
step; in a batch of 2,048 a common word can appear a hundred times. Without
clipping this run diverged to nan within half an epoch at learning rate 0.05. The
clip is applied per coordinate, to [−1, 1], before the contributions are summed:
it bounds individual contributions, not the accumulated row update. Options:
divide the gradient of the whole batch by the batch size, or divide each row's
accumulated gradient by the number of contributions of its index; neither
reproduces sequential SGD. Clipping is an optimization choice and can affect the
vectors that are learned.
:::

## The link between counting and predicting

::: {.lede}
Levy and Goldberg (2014): how skip-gram with negative sampling relates to matrix factorization.
:::

$$\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c = \mathrm{PMI}(w, c) - \log K$$

- The conditions: negatives come from the context marginal and every dot product can be chosen independently; then this is the optimal target for pairs with a positive count
- [Not every version of word2vec is identical to PPMI–SVD]{.hl}: shared low-dimensional vectors may not meet all the optima, and the 0.75 exponent changes the target
- For an explicit matrix: SPPMI $= \max(\mathrm{PMI} - \log K,\ 0)$

::: {.takeaway}
Levy et al. (2015): with matched hyperparameters, on the tasks they examined, the performance gap largely closes.
:::

::: {.src}
Baroni et al. 2014 · Levy & Goldberg 2014 · Levy, Goldberg & Dagan 2015
:::

::: {.notes}
For a while counting (LSA, PPMI+SVD) and predicting (word2vec) were seen as rival
approaches; Baroni, Dinu and Kruszewski (2014) compared the two and reported
better results for prediction-based methods. Then Levy and Goldberg showed the
relation.

Unobserved pairs: a pair whose positive count is zero can still be drawn as a
negative; the logistic optimum for its free score lies at the limit z → −∞. The
actual model works with finite parameters, shared low-dimensional vectors and a
finite number of updates, so it does not realize those limits exactly.

The −log K term: when K grows, with the other distributions held fixed, the free
dot-product targets shift down by the same constant. That is not in general
equivalent to adding the same vector to every word vector. Adding a constant to the
target matrix raises its rank by at most one; it can be represented with an extra
coordinate, but the same fit may not be preserved at a fixed d. The effect of K on
a task has to be assessed experimentally.

The caption of the chapter's figure: the PPMI–SVD route additionally clips at zero
and uses a squared loss; it is not expected to give the same vectors at low rank.

The hyperparameters in the follow-up paper: subsampling, context distribution
smoothing, dynamic windows. The lesson generalizes: when a new method beats an old
one, some of the improvement is the method and some is the tuning, and the split
is rarely reported.
:::

## Where the −log K comes from

::: {.lede}
Fix one pair and treat $z = \mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c$ as a free number. If the negatives are drawn from the context marginal $P(c)$, the pair's contribution to the objective **to be maximized** is:
:::

$$P(w,c)\,\log \sigma(z) \;+\; K\,P(w)P(c)\,\log \sigma(-z)$$

Set the derivative to zero, $P(w,c)\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr) = K\,P(w)P(c)\,\sigma(z)$, and solve:

$$z = \log \frac{P(w,c)}{K\,P(w)P(c)} = \mathrm{PMI}(w,c) - \log K$$

::: {.small-note}
The derivation assumes negatives drawn from $P(c)$ and a $z$ that can be chosen independently for every pair. In the actual model the dot products are built from shared vectors; SGNS minimizes a sampling-weighted logistic loss, PPMI–SVD the squared error of a clipped matrix. Both the losses and the targets can differ.
:::

::: {.notes}
The derivatives used: d/dz log σ(z) = 1 − σ(z) and d/dz log σ(−z) = −σ(z). Solve
for σ(z), then convert back through z = log(σ/(1 − σ)). The negative of the same
expression is the loss to be minimized.

The assumption that negatives come from the raw unigram distribution does not
match the code: word2vec draws them from f(c)^0.75, which gives PMI computed
against a smoothed context distribution. Levy, Goldberg and Dagan (2015) call this
context distribution smoothing and show it transfers to PPMI+SVD. So the 0.75
exponent changes which matrix the algorithm factorizes.

The statistical difference. Truncated SVD gives the best rank-d approximation in
Frobenius norm (Eckart–Young–Mirsky): an equal coefficient on the squared error of
every cell of the PPMI matrix. The zeros in PPMI cover pairs never observed and
also observed pairs whose PMI is zero or negative. The number of zeros does not by
itself show that most of the error or capacity goes to them. SGNS uses a logistic
loss under weights set by the positive pair frequencies and the negative-sampling
distribution; GloVe chooses yet another count-dependent weighting. Those
differences affect behaviour; they do not prove an unconditional advantage for any
method on rare words.

The choice weighs corpus size, the need for updates, memory, inspectability and
the target task together.

If the lecture is split in two, this is the place.
:::

## GloVe: counting, with a loss function

$$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{(w,c)\,:\,X_{wc} > 0} f(X_{wc}) \left(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c + b_w + b_c - \log X_{wc}\right)^2$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%" .compact}
- Accumulates co-occurrence counts explicitly; learns vectors and biases with a count-weighted squared error
- **Why $\log X$?** Counts span a wide range; logs turn ratios into differences
- **Why the biases?** They can model overall usage tendencies; [the dot products are not exactly PMI]{.hl}
- **Why $f$?** Down-weights rare pairs, capped at 1 for $x \geq 100$; zero counts are outside the sum
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
$f(x) = (x/x_{\max})^{3/4}$ for $x < x_{\max} = 100$, else 1

| $X_{wc}$ | $f(X_{wc})$ |
|--------:|------------:|
| 1       | 0.03        |
| 10      | 0.18        |
| 100     | 1.00        |
| 100,000 | 1.00        |
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Pennington et al. 2014
:::

::: {.notes}
GloVe accumulates the co-occurrence counts explicitly and learns the vectors with a
weighted loss defined on those counts; it combines a count-based representation
with gradient-based learning.

Input: a word–context co-occurrence table. The matrix C at the start of the chapter
added one for every pair in the window. In the original GloVe implementation
distant contexts can be counted with a lower weight, so the cells of X need not be
integers.

The loss: the sum v·u + b_w + b_c is asked to be close to the logarithm of the
positive co-occurrence count (weighted least squares). The two vector tables are
learned together, so this is not the same optimization problem as ordinary linear
regression.

Correct a common wrong intuition: GloVe uses "global statistics", but that table is
built from the same local windows word2vec sees. The difference is when the
learning happens: word2vec sees examples one at a time; GloVe counts and totals
them first, then optimizes against the totals.

The bias terms carry an intuition similar to the way PMI accounts for marginal
frequencies; but GloVe learns them jointly from the data, and they need not equal
the log row and column totals.

f: the weight does not grow without bound as the count grows; the squared residual
and the gradient can still be large. In its aim of controlling the influence of
frequent pairs it is related to subsampling; it is not the same operation. The
0.75 exponent in the two methods does different jobs too.
:::

## What a word is now

::: {.lede}
Pretrained GloVe: 400,000 vectors, 100 dimensions, trained on Wikipedia 2014 + Gigaword 5 (6 billion tokens).
:::

| query    | nearest neighbours                                  | what it shows                          |
|:---------|:----------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|
| `king`   | prince 0.77, queen 0.75, son 0.70                   | —                                      |
| `pump`   | pumps 0.84, pumping 0.77, pumped 0.71               | `pumps` is a neighbour, not an orthogonal axis |
| `turkey` | ankara 0.75, turkish 0.72, greece 0.71              | words about the country stand out      |
| `python` | monty 0.69, php 0.59, perl 0.58, flipper 0.51       | neighbours from different usages together |
| `bank`   | banks 0.81, banking 0.75, credit 0.70               | words about finance stand out          |

::: {.takeaway}
The defining limitation of a static embedding: [one vector per word form, whatever the context]{.hl}. That limitation is one of the important reasons for the context-dependent token representations of Chapter 7.
:::

::: {.notes}
For the rest of the chapter we use GloVe's pretrained vectors as an easily obtained
example of a static representation.

`king` starts −0.323, −0.876, 0.22, 0.253, … and has norm 6.118. No labels such as
"royalty" or "gender" were assigned to these coordinates in advance. Some
coordinates may turn out to be related to particular properties; such readings
depend on the chosen representation and are usually not preserved when the
coordinate system changes.

For `python`, neighbours related to the comedy troupe (`monty`, `cleese`) and to
programming languages (`php`, `perl`) appear together. Which usage the `flipper`
result comes from cannot be determined from this list alone. The lists show that a
single vector can carry the influence of different usages together; they are not
an inventory of all the senses.

The Turkish example: *yüz* can mean *face*, the number *hundred*, or the
imperative *swim*. A static table gives that form a single vector; the different
usages influence what is learned, but the result is not an explicitly computed
mean of those senses. Querying the vector by itself cannot select the sense in use
in a sentence; a model that processes it together with the surrounding words can
make use of the context.
:::

## king − man + woman ≈ queen?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Inputs removed

::: {.roomy}
| word     | cosine |
|:---------|--------:|
| queen    | 0.7699  |
| monarch  | 0.6843  |
| throne   | 0.6756  |
| daughter | 0.6595  |
| princess | 0.6521  |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### The same scores, unfiltered

::: {.roomy}
| word      | cosine |
|:----------|--------:|
| **king**  | 0.8361  |
| queen     | 0.7699  |
| monarch   | 0.6843  |
| throne    | 0.6756  |
| daughter  | 0.6595  |
:::
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
`gensim` normalizes the inputs and removes them from the candidates. With the scores fixed, the unfiltered nearest neighbour is [`king`]{.hl}; `queen` is first only without the inputs. The candidate set is part of the task.
:::

::: {.notes}
The result that made embeddings famous outside NLP. It indicates that some
relations can be represented by similar vector differences. An exact parallelogram
is sufficient for the arithmetic to produce the `queen` vector itself; it is not
necessary for `queen` to be selected as the nearest neighbour. Nor can we conclude
from this example that the differences consist of a single gender direction only.

The rule of the comparison: to see the effect of the filter alone, hold the scores
fixed. The code takes the scores for the whole vocabulary with
`most_similar(..., topn=None)` and ranks them with two candidate sets. The
unfiltered `king` is the result of an unrestricted neighbour search; it does not
show that the expected answer to the analogy is `king`.

If the inputs are added without normalizing them first, the scores change a little
(`king` 0.8552, `queen` 0.7834); the top of the ranking stays the same.
:::

## Evaluating analogies

- The scoring is called **3CosAdd**: it combines the candidate's cosines with the three inputs using two plus signs and one minus. Excluding the inputs is a separate evaluation rule. **3CosMul** (Levy and Goldberg 2014) gives better results in some evaluations
- Linzen (2016): a nearest-neighbour baseline that ignores the relation reaches a large share of the reported accuracy in some categories
- In five of the book's eight selected examples the unfiltered nearest candidate is an input; that proportion does not measure analogy accuracy in general
- `mice − mouse + goose`: the expected `geese` is third in the unfiltered list and second, behind `cows`, once the inputs are removed
- `madrid − spain + germany`: `munich` comes ahead of `berlin`. [The expected answer is not first; that does not prove the model carries no information about the capital relation]{.hl}

::: {.notes}
The scoring method and the candidate filter should be reported separately.

Linzen's point: the headline analogy number measures neighbourhood structure as
much as it measures a relation. On this example the baseline would be wrong —
`king`'s nearest neighbour is `prince` (0.77) — but `queen` is already the
second-nearest neighbour (0.75) before any arithmetic. Nissim, van Noord and van
der Goot (2020) show that excluding the input words can also affect how bias
analogies are read; the model, the normalization and the candidate set a result
was obtained with should be stated together.

The eight analogies in the book's interactive tool (real GloVe results; scores
computed the same way as in the code above): king − man + woman,
paris − france + italy, walking − walk + swim, bigger − big + small,
madrid − spain + germany, windows − microsoft + google, mice − mouse + goose,
einstein − physics + biology. Unfiltered top results: `walking − walk + swim` →
swim 0.8385; `windows − microsoft + google` → windows 0.8330;
`einstein − physics + biology` → einstein 0.7982. `paris − france + italy` gives
rome 0.8190.

The chapter also projects thirty words to two dimensions. Read it with care: those
are the first two principal components of those thirty vectors, not of all
400,000, and they keep only 37.5% of the variance. The GloVe similarities in this
section are computed with the original 100-dimensional vectors; the projection is
for visualization only.
:::

## Turkish makes more than twice the word forms

::: {.lede}
Two Wikipedia samples of comparable size:
:::

|                                         | Turkish   | English   |
|:----------------------------------------|----------:|----------:|
| tokens                                  | 1,458,213 | 1,828,840 |
| distinct word forms                     | 138,578   | 78,140    |
| forms seen after 1 million tokens       | 112,644   | 52,347    |
| forms seen exactly once (hapax)         | 50.0%     | 46.7%     |
| test tokens outside the training vocabulary | 7.33% | 4.72%     |

::: {.takeaway}
`ev`, `evim`, `evimde`, `evimdeki`, `evlerimizdekiler` are five separate vocabulary entries. [In the held-out Turkish portion about one token in fourteen falls outside the training vocabulary.]{.hl} The numbers belong to one sample and one tokenization choice.
:::

::: {.notes}
Out-of-vocabulary (OOV): a form that is not in the model's word vocabulary. It may
never have been seen in training, or it may have been dropped for a reason such as
a frequency threshold. For a form that is not in the table no row can be fetched
directly; the `gensim` lookup used here raises a KeyError, and other systems may
use a special unknown-unit representation.

Vocabulary growth: Turkish 45,688 at 250k, 73,435 at 500k, 97,412 at 750k, 112,644
at 1 million, 126,389 at 1.25 million; English 22,869, 34,016, 42,854, 52,347,
60,178. New forms keep arriving over the range shown.

Hapax: 69,296 of 138,578 types in Turkish; 36,503 of 78,140 in English. That half
the types occur once does not mean half the vectors are learned from a single
example: a frequency filter can leave those types out, and a single token produces
several context pairs.

Out-of-vocabulary rate (train on 90%, test on the last 10%): 7.33% of tokens and
28.99% of types in Turkish; 4.72% and 23.29% in English. The rate also depends on
how the held-out portion is chosen; it changes on another sample.
:::

## fastText: a word is built from its pieces

$$\mathbf{v}_w = \mathbf{1}_{\{w \in \mathcal{V}\}}\,\mathbf{z}_w + \sum_{g \in G(w)} \mathbf{z}_g$$

- The separate whole-word component exists only for words in the vocabulary; an out-of-vocabulary word is built from its subword components
- Shared character n-grams receive updates from examples in different words: `<pu` inside `pump`, `pumps`, `pumped`, `pumping`, `punch` … [Not every piece is learned from plentiful data]{.hl}; the n-grams are mapped to a fixed number of hash buckets

**pumps**, seen in training: [**&lt;pu**]{.chip} [**pum**]{.chip} [**ump**]{.chip} [mps]{.chip} [ps&gt;]{.chip} [&lt;pumps&gt;]{.chip}

**pumpage**, never seen: [**&lt;pu**]{.chip} [**pum**]{.chip} [**ump**]{.chip} [mpa]{.chip} [pag]{.chip} [age]{.chip} [ge&gt;]{.chip} — word2vec: `KeyError`

::: {.small-note}
Drawn with 3-grams so it stays readable; fastText's default is every n-gram of length 3 to 6, so a real `pumpage` decomposes into 22 pieces, not 7.
:::

::: {.notes}
fastText (Bojanowski et al. 2017) does not treat a word as atomic: it represents a
word as the sum of its character n-grams plus, if the word is in the vocabulary, a
vector for the whole word. V is the whole-word vocabulary and G(w) the multiset of
the selected character n-grams.

The bold pieces are shared. `pumpage` has no whole-word vector; only the n-grams
carry it. That a vector can be produced for an out-of-vocabulary word does not by
itself show that the vector is semantically reliable.

Sum and mean: the sum in the paper and the mean that `fastText` and `gensim`
compute give the same direction for a non-zero word vector; word-to-word cosines
are identical. Do not read that as saying a sum or a mean in training, or in
combining words into a document vector, is equivalent under all conditions.

The angle brackets mark the start and the end of the word; they separate the
boundary form of a letter sequence from its word-internal form. That does not by
itself analyse stems or suffixes. The default example in the book's tool is
`kitaplarımızdaki` against `kitaplar`.

The trade-off: shared n-gram vectors tie together the representations of words
spelled alike. That can provide morphological generalization, and it can also
create unwanted closeness between unrelated words. The whole-word component of an
in-vocabulary word can learn information apart from that effect.
:::

## What subwords buy

::: {.lede}
Out-of-vocabulary words: two Turkish forms the Turkish Wikipedia sample never contained, then two typos. word2vec raises `KeyError`; fastText still gives a vector:
:::

| word               | fastText's nearest neighbours                            |
|:-------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| `kitaplarımızdaki` | kitapları 0.91, kitapların 0.91, kitaplıkları 0.90       |
| `bilgisayarcılık`  | bilgisayara 0.96, bilgisayarlı 0.96, bilgisayar 0.96     |
| `philosphy`        | philosophy 0.96, philosophie 0.95, philosophies 0.94     |
| `governmentt`      | government 0.98, governments 0.94, governmental 0.93     |

::: {.takeaway}
Shared character pieces help with some typos as well: in these examples the out-of-vocabulary forms get vectors close to the expected words. [That result is not guaranteed for every typo.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
The two Turkish rows come from word2vec and fastText trained on the same Turkish
Wikipedia sample: both words are missing from both vocabularies and word2vec raises
KeyError on each. The last two rows are typos; they are not in the vocabulary
either.

Fourth neighbours, for completeness: `kitaplarımızdaki` → kitaplarda 0.90;
`bilgisayarcılık` → bilgisayarı 0.96; `philosphy` → philology 0.94;
`governmentt` → governs 0.91.
:::

## What subwords cost

| query                                | fastText                              | word2vec                                     |
|:-------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|
| `kitap` (book)                       | kitapta 0.96, kitaba 0.95, kitab 0.94 | eseri 0.81, makale 0.80, eseriyle 0.80       |
| `yaz` (summer; also "write")         | yao 0.78, yağ 0.77, yağdı 0.77        | kış 0.86, olimpiyatları 0.84, aylarında 0.83 |
| cosine of `kitap`–`kitle`            | 0.667                                 | 0.446                                        |

- `kitap`: inflections or *semantic* neighbours? It depends on your task. `yaz`: spelling neighbours come to the front in fastText
- The ratio of 0.667 to 0.446 cannot be read as "half again as similar": the cosine distributions of the two spaces can differ

::: {.takeaway}
fastText is a strong candidate where out-of-vocabulary forms and inflection matter. [Character sharing can also create unwanted closeness: evaluate by coverage and task performance.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Character n-grams make it possible to share some stem and suffix patterns without
an explicit morphological analyser. In return, the representations of words that
are spelled alike but mean different things can move closer together too.

For `kitap`, word2vec returns semantic neighbours such as `eseri` (his/her work)
and `makale` (article). For `yaz`, the word2vec neighbours reflect the seasonal
usage more (`kış` winter, `olimpiyatları`, `gündönümü` solstice); fastText returns
`yao`, `yağ` (oil), `yayoi`, `yay` (bow).

The rule: do not accept or reject the method unconditionally according to word
length. Compare the score distributions of unrelated or hard-negative pairs as
well. The idea shared with BPE (Chapter 2) is to benefit from rare wholes through
their pieces; the mechanism differs: BPE determines the tokenization units,
fastText builds a word vector by combining overlapping character n-gram vectors.
:::

## Documents as vectors

::: {.lede}
Chapter 2's four 20 Newsgroups categories, same split, same logistic regression on top:
:::

| representation                   | accuracy | dimensions |
|:---------------------------------|---------:|-----------:|
| TF-IDF (Ch. 2 baseline)          | **0.853** | 32,014    |
| averaged GloVe                   | 0.820    | 100        |
| idf-weighted averaged GloVe      | 0.822    | 100        |
| doc2vec (PV-DBOW, 40 epochs)     | 0.839    | 100        |
| averaged GloVe + doc2vec         | 0.845    | 200        |

::: {.takeaway}
On this split TF-IDF has the highest accuracy. [In the paired test its gap to averaged GloVe is hard to explain by chance: 135 documents against 84, p = 0.0007.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.small-note}
The standard error of one accuracy (≈ 0.010) is not that of the difference between two models. The two GloVe averages: 66 against 63 (p = 0.86). No such calculation for the doc2vec rows: their predictions cannot be reproduced exactly.
:::

::: {.notes}
The plain mean: the average of the word vectors in a document. The function
expects a list of tokens; out-of-vocabulary tokens are skipped, and a document with
no vector stays a zero row (79 of the 2,327 training documents, 65 of the 1,550
test documents). In the IDF-weighted mean, IDF is computed from the training
documents only.

doc2vec (Le and Mikolov 2014) assigns a learnable vector to the document id as
well; negative sampling or hierarchical softmax can be used. PV-DM predicts the
target word from the document vector and context words; PV-DBOW predicts words
sampled from the document from the document vector alone. Lau and Baldwin (2016)
found that PV-DBOW can also be strong and computationally convenient on the tasks
they examined; in `gensim`, `dm=1` (the default) is PV-DM and `dm=0` is PV-DBOW.
On reproducibility: the final version (v7) of Mesnil et al. reports 88.73% with
paragraph vectors alone, against the 92.58% IMDB accuracy of the original paper,
and says 92.6% appeared only when the data were not shuffled. That is the result
of one particular replication.

A new document: the model's word and output parameters are held fixed and the new
document vector is estimated with a few optimization steps; that requires the
trained model.

McNemar's test compares the counts, in the two directions, of documents that one
model gets right and the other gets wrong. The Bonferroni threshold for three
comparisons is 0.017. `infer_vector` derives its starting vector from a hash value
that changes in every Python session, so the doc2vec predictions behind the table
cannot be reproduced exactly; with a fixed hash the notebook finds 0.830–0.836.

A reduction in the number of coordinates is not the same ratio of memory saved;
sparse storage, running time and the search method have to be measured as well.

SIF (Arora, Liang and Ma 2017): weights a/(a + p(w)) that depend on word frequency,
and removal of a common dominant component. Not the same method as the
IDF-weighted mean; a separate baseline that can be compared on tasks such as
sentence similarity.
:::

## What averaging destroys

- Coverage: GloVe covers 98.6% of the *tokens* and 84.5% of the *types*; the uncovered forms are 1.4% of the token mass, and averaging leaves them out

```text
a = "the pump failed and the valve is fine"
b = "the valve failed and the pump is fine"
```

::: {.fragment}
- Cosine of the two averaged vectors: **1.0000**. The same tokens occur the same number of times, so the unordered mean is [mathematically the same vector]{.hl}
- In floating point the order of addition produces small differences: `np.allclose` is `True`, the bit-level comparison is `False` (largest difference $1.2 \times 10^{-7}$)
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Averaging does not keep the word order that determines which part failed: chapter 2's bag-of-words problem, now in 100 dimensions. Word order needs a model that reads the sequence (Chapters 6 and 7).
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask the room for the cosine before revealing (one click).

Coverage in numbers: 23,395 of 27,681 types.

The chapter's code averages the GloVe vectors of the split sentences with np.mean
and prints the cosine: 1.0000 and "identical: True". "Identical" there is the
result of `np.allclose`; bit-level equality is not guaranteed in every
implementation.

Word order belongs to Chapter 6 (Language Models) and Chapter 7 (Transformers and
Attention).
:::

## In this space, cosine reflects relatedness more than similarity

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.roomy}
| pair                    | cosine    |
|:------------------------|----------:|
| `good` – `bad`          | 0.770     |
| `hot` – `cold`          | 0.725     |
| `increase` – `decrease` | **0.881** |
| `cat` – `dog`           | **0.880** |
| `cat` – `car`           | 0.311     |
| `teacher` – `student`   | 0.808     |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
- The antonym pair gets a high cosine too — the **antonym problem**; the gap between 0.881 and 0.880 is not a meaningful ordering
- The model sees a word's *surroundings*: `hot` and `cold` appear next to the same words
- In this space cosine mostly reflects *relatedness*
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
[Do not read the raw cosine of static vectors directly as a measure of sentiment or polarity.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
The road map of the geometry part: distributional relatedness, the distribution of
directions and the effect of frequency; then the arbitrariness of the coordinate
system and how consistent different training runs are.

The practical cost of the antonym problem: a system searching for "hot" may return
documents containing "cold" among its most similar results. Task-specific labels,
for contradiction or synonymy for example, can help a model learn the distinction
and generalize to pairs not seen directly in training; success depends on the
coverage of the data and on the training objective.

Steck, Ekanadham and Kallus (2024): in certain linear matrix-factorization models
the cosines can change while the training predictions are preserved. Cosine is not
a scale of meaning independent of the learned representation. The distribution
over random pairs gives a useful basis for comparison; assessing similarity for a
task additionally requires labelled examples. Do not treat 0.8 in two models as
equivalent.

Evaluation data measure different relations as well: WordSim-353 (Finkelstein et
al. 2002) contains judgements that also reflect broad semantic relatedness;
SimLex-999 (Hill et al. 2015), developed later, aims to separate similarity from
relatedness.
:::

## The space is not isotropic

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="46%"}
4,000 unit vectors from the top 50,000 GloVe words

::: {.roomy}
| statistic                     | value  |
|:------------------------------|-------:|
| mean cosine, random pairs     | 0.029  |
| standard deviation            | 0.119  |
| pairs with cosine > 0         | 56.9%  |
| norm of the mean vector       | 0.171  |
| mean cosine after centring    | −0.000 |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="54%" .compact}
- **Isotropic** = the same in every direction. **Anisotropic** = not; a shift toward a common direction is one form, [not a requirement]{.hl}
- Mean cosine and mean-vector norm are one piece of evidence: $\bar{c} = (n\lVert\bar{v}\rVert^2 - 1)/(n-1) \approx 0.029$
- Random pairs show how unusual a score is; a fixed 0.3 does not by itself mean a semantic relation
- Centring removes the mean direction, not all anisotropy. *All-but-the-top* (Mu, Bhat and Viswanath 2018): measure on the task
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Explain the word first. Picture every vector as an arrow leaving a common centre:
in an isotropic space the arrows spread evenly in all directions. A shift toward a
common direction is not required for anisotropy: the vectors can concentrate in the
two opposite directions of one axis and still have a zero mean.

The null: for independent unit vectors drawn uniformly in d dimensions the angles
concentrate near 90°, with mean cosine 0 and variance 1/d. The 56.9% proves little
on its own: the 8 million pairs come from 4,000 vectors, so they are not
independent observations.

The values in this sample are consistent with a shared mean direction; they do not
by themselves show that the whole space is squeezed into a narrow cone. That the
mean cosine after centring should be exactly zero is not a general identity. The
results belong to the sample drawn from the first 50,000 words. Centring does not
make the covariance spherical either.

Ethayarajh (2019) observes strong anisotropy in certain layers of the contextual
models he examines; do not read that as a fixed ordering for every method of
contextual representation.

The histogram in the book: in this sample, centring brings the mean cosine close
to zero.
:::

## Frequency leaks in; your domain lives in the tail

::: {.lede}
Frequent words have longer vectors on average: mean norm 6.19 for the top 100 words, 3.62 for ranks 100,000–400,000.
:::

| term         | rank    | nearest neighbours                             |
|:-------------|--------:|:-----------------------------------------------|
| `water`      | 430     | natural 0.70, dry 0.68, salt 0.68              |
| `turbine`    | 15,747  | turbines 0.80, compressor 0.78, generator 0.72 |
| `cavitation` | 109,044 | aliasing 0.56, barotrauma 0.54, attenuation 0.54 |
| `impeller`   | 124,835 | armature 0.62, evaporator 0.61, nozzle 0.60    |
| `eutectic`   | 159,022 | azeotrope 0.61, azeotropic 0.55, tiwai 0.54    |

::: {.takeaway}
[Evaluate domain terms separately.]{.hl} Neighbour lists are a good first check; choose the method by comparing pretrained, domain-adapted and subword representations with task metrics.
:::

::: {.notes}
Norm and direction. The table shows that the norm can be related to frequency; it
does not show that cosine is the best measure for every task. Cosine leaves the
norm out and compares directions; Euclidean distance is affected by both. For
unit-norm vectors ‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2cos(a, b), so the two measures give the same
ranking. Whether keeping the norm or removing it helps is assessed on the task.

Mean norm by frequency rank: 0–100: 6.19; 100–1,000: 5.85; 1,000–10,000: 5.45;
10,000–100,000: 4.99; 100,000–400,000: 3.62. Spearman(log rank, norm) over the top
100k words: −0.313. That is a trend across bands.

Raw dot products and Euclidean distance can be affected by differences in norm; a
model that takes unnormalized vectors can make use of that information, and how
far it does so depends on its objective and parameters.

Neighbour lists: the `turbine` neighbours look related to equipment and energy
systems. For the `cavitation` and `eutectic` lists, which relations are useful for
the task has to be judged with domain knowledge; being related within the same
physical process is not the same as being synonymous. No general quality ranking
can be drawn from these short lists.
:::

## Arbitrary coordinates, variable runs {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Same corpus, same settings, two seeds (`text8`, 6,794,527 tokens)

::: {.roomy}
| measurement | value |
|:--|--:|
| same word, raw coordinates: mean cosine | −0.016 |
| after orthogonal (Procrustes) alignment | +0.951 |
| top-10 neighbour overlap, 1,000 most frequent | 62.2% |
| top-10 neighbour overlap, 1,000 rarest | 46.6% |
| largest cosine change under an orthogonal map | 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%" .compact}
- Multiply both tables by the same orthogonal $R$: $(WR)(UR)^\top = WU^\top$ — [every coordinate changes, no dot product does]{.hl}
- A coordinate's meaning in one run may not survive a change of coordinates
- +0.951: the coordinates explain much of the difference, not all — the neighbour overlaps show local differences remain
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
Same corpus + different seed → geometrically different, functionally similar spaces. Do not argue from one neighbour list of one run.
:::

::: {.notes}
The numbers are the chapter's measurement: word2vec trained twice on the same text8
slice with the same settings, changing only the seed (gensim 4.4, vocabulary
18,677). `workers=1` reduces the variability that comes from thread ordering; exact
reproduction also needs the data order, PYTHONHASHSEED, the library versions and
the environment to be fixed.

The transformation: multiply every vector by the same random orthogonal matrix;
all of `king`'s coordinates change and the `king`–`queen` cosine stays at 0.6826.
Orthogonal Procrustes alignment may include a reflection; do not call it "just a
rotation".

When comparing different periods or corpora, align on shared anchor words that are
as stable as possible, and take care not to absorb the change under study into the
alignment.

Stability: even for the most frequent words about four of ten neighbours differ
between the two runs; for the rarest, more than half. If a neighbourhood matters,
train with a few seeds and look at which neighbours come back every time.
:::

## Bias is in the data, and the geometry records it

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
Projection onto `woman` − `man`

| word           | projection |
|:---------------|--------:|
| `homemaker`    | +0.363  |
| `nurse`        | +0.329  |
| `receptionist` | +0.281  |
| `teacher`      | +0.152  |
| `doctor`       | +0.109  |
| `scientist`    | −0.046  |
| `programmer`   | −0.083  |
| `engineer`     | −0.123  |
:::

::: {.column width="60%" .compact}
The sign shows the direction of the projection on the chosen axis; it does not measure all of social bias.

1. **Usually not a training error** — associations in the data carry over into the geometry; what you measure depends on the corpus, the model and the axis
2. **It can carry over into decisions** — depending on the downstream objective, inputs and decision rule; evaluate the application's outputs too
3. **One intervention does not remove every indicator** — [gender-related information can remain]{.hl} (Gonen & Goldberg 2019)
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Bolukbasi et al. 2016 · Caliskan et al. 2017 · Gonen & Goldberg 2019
:::

::: {.notes}
The chapter lists the words in a different order (doctor, nurse, engineer, teacher,
programmer, homemaker, scientist, receptionist); the slide sorts them by
projection. Positive means the `woman` side.

Bolukbasi et al. (2016) estimate a direction, or a subspace, from several defining
word pairs and not from a single pair; the single-pair calculation here is a
teaching simplification. Their method includes neutralize and equalize steps for
selected words. Caliskan, Bryson and Narayanan (2017), with WEAT, find relations
similar to various human association patterns in the word sets they examine.
Reaction times in people and relations between vectors are different measurements;
do not read the effect sizes as the same quantity.

What Gonen and Goldberg show: a fall in the chosen metric does not show that all
the related structure has been erased.

Ask the room the chapter's intuition check: is a model that shows no bias on this
test unbiased? No. The test measures one direction defined by one word pair.
Passing a single fairness metric is evidence only about the kind of bias that
metric can detect.
:::

## How do you know an embedding is any good?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%" .compact}
- **Intrinsic**: does the space agree with human judgements — similarity ratings, analogies? Fast; needs no real task
- **Extrinsic**: does it improve the thing you care about? Slow, but [the evaluation that measures the contribution directly]{.hl}
- The same GloVe vectors: WordSim-353 Spearman **0.533**; SimLex-999 **0.296**. The coverage of the sets and their kinds of judgement differ too; the gap cannot be explained by antonymy alone
- Intrinsic scores are useful for comparing properties and eliminating candidates; for choosing what to deploy, performance and cost on the target task decide (Schnabel et al. 2015)
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Google analogies: **0.633** overall

| category                  | accuracy |
|:--------------------------|---------:|
| capital-common-countries  | 0.939    |
| capital-world             | 0.889    |
| nationality-adjective     | 0.879    |
| family                    | 0.816    |
| city-in-state             | 0.308    |
| opposite                  | 0.201    |
| currency                  | 0.152    |
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation measure different aspects of a representation.

The Google analogy set: 19,544 questions in 14 categories. The per-category
breakdown shows differences the overall score hides. Those differences can be
affected by corpus coverage, the type of relation and the scoring method; they do
not by themselves prove which cause dominates. Report the overall accuracy
together with the category scores, the coverage and simple baselines. Even the low
categories are far above random choice from a set of 300,000 candidates.

The other categories: gram1-adjective-to-adverb 0.244; gram3-comparative 0.791;
gram4-superlative 0.543; gram5-present-participle 0.695; gram7-past-tense 0.554;
gram8-plural 0.720; gram9-plural-verbs 0.584. The "gram6-"/"gram2-" prefixes are
dropped from the category names on the slide.

A gensim detail: the default is restrict_vocab = 300,000. In the word-pair
evaluation, pairs containing a word outside that limit are skipped; no search for a
candidate answer takes place. In the analogies both the questions covered and the
candidate vocabulary are limited.
:::

## The same dataset, different evaluated examples {.smaller}

|                    | GloVe · 6 billion tokens | from scratch · 6.8 million tokens |
|:-------------------|:-------------------------|:----------------------------------|
| WordSim-353        | 0.533 · 0.0% skipped     | **0.627** · 11.9% skipped          |
| the 311 common pairs | 0.549                  | 0.627                              |
| Analogies, questions scored | 0.633 · 19,486  | 0.200 · 9,282                      |
| Analogies, all 19,544 questions | 0.631       | 0.095                              |

- WordSim: the small model is ahead on the common pairs too — here coverage does not close the gap. Analogies: counting skipped questions as wrong (`dummy4unknown=True`) halves the small model's score
- All 58 questions GloVe skips contain `denar`: in the vocabulary (rank 394,434), outside the default limit of 300,000

::: {.takeaway}
[Give the coverage and the number of examples scored together with the score.]{.hl} The direction of the effect of skipped examples depends on which examples are skipped.
:::

::: {.notes}
The same dataset name does not mean the same evaluated examples.

WordSim-353: the small model's vocabulary is 18,677 words; 11.9% of the pairs are
skipped. On the 311 pairs (88.1%) both models cover, GloVe scores 0.549 and the
NumPy model 0.627. On the 42 pairs the small model skips, GloVe's correlation is
0.473; those pairs are somewhat harder than average for GloVe, but the gap does
not close. This result on a single relatedness set does not show the small model
is better in general; the analogy numbers say the opposite.

Analogies: the default dummy4unknown=False skips questions containing an
out-of-coverage word. dummy4unknown=True counts skipped questions as wrong; it
does not give the model vectors for unknown words. GloVe gets 12,334 of the 19,544
questions right, the NumPy model 1,852. The candidate vocabulary, case sensitivity
and the input filter should be reported the same way.

The rule: do not compare scores computed on different subsets of examples as if
they had the same coverage.
:::

## Choosing between them

| method         | reach for it when                                               | watch for                                                        |
|:---------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| **PPMI + SVD** | you want to inspect the steps of the computation, or set up a count-based baseline on a modest vocabulary | sparse count matrix, low-rank factors and solver memory; no row for out-of-vocabulary forms |
| **word2vec**   | you want to learn word vectors from a domain corpus — measuring against fastText | performance depends on sampling, settings and coverage; the final vectors alone are not enough to continue training |
| **GloVe**      | you want a quick start with released vectors that cover the language and domain you need | training needs the co-occurrence data prepared; coverage of a released vocabulary varies with language and domain |
| **fastText**   | the OOV rate, inflectional variety or spelling variability is high | the subword table needs extra memory; similar spelling can create unwanted closeness (`kitap`/`kitle` 0.667) |

::: {.small-note}
Evaluate the coverage gain on task performance and hard negatives (the measurement in Chapter 4). For documents: on the single split of this experiment none of the dense methods beat the TF-IDF row; that finding does not cover every classification or retrieval task.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four methods, all producing a dense vector per word, all comparable by cosine. The
differences matter only in specific circumstances.

Counting and predicting as engineering. Memory: large corpora need a sparse
co-occurrence matrix, the low-rank vectors and the solver's working memory; in a
streaming SGNS implementation the two tables take O(Vd) space, and the sampler and
buffers need memory too. The chapter's NumPy example stores every pair, so its
memory also depends on corpus size. Reproducibility: for SVD the solver, the
environment and (if randomized) the seed are fixed; the signs of singular vectors
and the choice of basis in equal-singular-value subspaces are not unique. For SGNS
the seed, data order, thread count and environment are controlled. New data: counts
can be updated incrementally; SGNS training can continue if the two tables, the
vocabulary and the training state have been kept.

Documents: averaged word vectors need no extra training of a document
representation; they lose word order and syntactic relations and do not reliably
keep the scope of negation. doc2vec gave higher accuracy than averaged GloVe in
this experiment (0.839 against 0.820); the uncertainty of the difference has to be
measured with a paired evaluation. Chapter 4 (A Representation Bake-Off) runs
the comparison with a different language, domain and amount of data, along a
learning curve.
:::

## Applications in production systems {.smaller}

- **Airbnb search ranking** — listing embeddings from skip-gram on click sessions: session = sentence, listing = word, the booked listing as global context (Grbovic & Cheng 2018)
- **YouTube recommendations** — the embeddings of watched videos and of search tokens are averaged separately and passed, with other user information, to a deep candidate-generation network; the network's output is the user representation (Covington et al. 2016)
- **Item2vec** — skip-gram-like objectives can be applied to item co-occurrences such as purchase baskets; not every `*2vec` uses the same objective (Barkan & Koenigstein 2016)
- **fastText for classification** — the vectors of word and *word* n-gram features with a linear output layer on top (Joulin et al. 2017); not the same unit as character n-grams
- **Retrieval with vectors** — some of the systems in Chapters 19 and 20 represent texts as vectors; RAG can also be built on lexical or hybrid retrieval

::: {.takeaway}
[An embedding layer maps discrete identities to learnable continuous vectors.]{.hl} What is differentiated is not the identity itself but the vector parameters that stand for it.
:::

::: {.notes}
word2vec's legacy is not the "word": it is the idea of learning an embedding for
any discrete entity from co-occurrence.

Airbnb: deployed to production search and reported as a substantial booking gain.
fastText for classification: a baseline worth testing for its balance of speed and
accuracy; training time and performance depend on the data and the settings.

In a standard table every identity has its own row; the shared training objective
makes those rows be learned in a related space. In structures such as fastText
there is real parameter sharing as well, through the subword pieces. The resulting
vectors can be used in downstream models with a suitable input dimension and
structure.
:::

## What static embeddings cannot do {.smaller}

| limitation                   | evidence from this chapter                          | common way to address or mitigate it |
|:-------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------|
| One static vector per form   | `python`: neighbours from different usages | representations computed from context (Ch. 7) |
| Unordered combination        | same tokens, different order → same mean | sequence models (Ch. 6) |
| Vocabulary coverage          | `KeyError`; OOV 7.3% on the Turkish sample | subword representations |
| Similarity and oppositeness mixed | `increase`/`decrease` 0.881 | evaluation with task-suited labels |
| Uneven directions            | mean cosine 0.029 (top-50,000 sample) | testing centring on the task |
| Rare / out-of-domain words   | neighbours of some domain terms | domain evaluation, adaptation |
| Social associations          | `homemaker` +0.363 | several metrics; testing interventions |

::: {.takeaway}
A static embedding is a type-level lookup table: word form → one vector. [A contextual model computes the token's representation from the surroundings it can access.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
A static table maps a word form to the same vector; different usages can influence
that vector, but no sense is selected anew in each sentence. In a contextual model
the surroundings depend on the attention pattern: bidirectional models use both
sides, causal models only the preceding tokens they are allowed to see.

The second row is a different problem: word order is about how individual vectors
are combined into a sentence or document vector, not about the vectors themselves.

ELMo (Peters et al. 2018) was an important turning point in the spread of this
approach, using the internal states of a bidirectional language model as word
representations that change with context. The idea of contextual representation
existed earlier; ELMo is an effective example of producing general-purpose,
transferable representations from it.
:::

## Intuition check 1 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Your embedding has 300 dimensions. Why 300 and not 30 or 3,000?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- There is no universal optimum at 300
- With fewer dimensions the capacity of the representation can be limited; with more, memory and computation cost rise, and how well detail learned from little data generalizes is assessed separately
- A low dimension does not force unrelated words onto the same point; a high dimension does not necessarily produce noise
- GloVe 50 → 100 dimensions: WordSim 0.503 → 0.533, SimLex 0.263 → 0.296, analogy 0.464 → 0.633
- [On the real task, compare the dimension options for performance, memory and latency]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Give students a minute before revealing (one click).

The dimension sweeps in the GloVe paper (Pennington et al. 2014) show that, in
particular experiments, the gain can slow down as the dimension grows. That can
make a few hundred dimensions a good starting range; it is not evidence for a
universal default.
:::

## Intuition check 2 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Why negative sampling instead of a softmax over the vocabulary?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Scoring cost: about $O(Vd)$ per pair for the full softmax, $O((K+1)d)$ with $K$ negatives. The sampler has a cost too: the binary search used here takes $O(\log V)$ per sample
- Not merely a faster computation: [the training objective changes]{.hl}
- With $q = P(c)$ and free dot products the target is shifted PMI (Levy and Goldberg 2014)
- Hierarchical softmax: a normalized probability through decisions along a tree path; about $O(d \log V)$ for a balanced tree
:::

::: {.notes}
Hierarchical softmax is not standard in modern large language models; you can meet
it as an option in classic word2vec training.
:::

## Intuition check 3 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
You have 50,000 support tickets in Turkish. word2vec or fastText?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Measure first: the number of tokens and types in the tickets and the OOV rate on a train/test split
- The inflectional variety of Turkish makes fastText a strong candidate; but [the 7.3% OOV rate on Wikipedia is not a lower bound for support tickets]{.hl} — the vocabulary of a narrow, repetitive domain can be smaller, too
- Compare the two under the same preprocessing and evaluation conditions
- Weigh the coverage gain together with unwanted spelling-based closeness (`kitap`/`kitle`)
:::

::: {.notes}
The good answer to this question is a measurement plan, not the name of a method.
:::

## Intuition check 4 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Cosine similarity between two documents' averaged vectors is 0.95. Are they about the same thing?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- That does not follow from 0.95 alone. Averaging loses order; opposite relations can be built from the same words
- We measured it: over the chapter's 2,248 Newsgroups documents, random pairs have mean cosine **0.944** and median 0.961; **65.6%** of the pairs are above 0.95
- Even among pairs from different newsgroups, 63.8%
- [Evaluate the decision threshold with pairs labelled as similar, unrelated and hard negatives]{.hl}; a percentile is not by itself a probability of semantic equivalence
:::

::: {.notes}
The shared component does not have to grow under averaging: the independent,
varying contributions shrink and the relative effect of the common direction can
rise. In this corpus 0.95 is below what a typical random pair scores.
:::

## Intuition check 5 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Should you fine-tune pretrained embeddings on your own corpus, or train from scratch?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Look at two axes: the size of your domain corpus, and how well the pretrained vocabulary covers your terms
- Small corpus, high coverage: use the pretrained vectors. Small corpus, low coverage: a subword model or a contextual encoder
- Medium–large corpus: *test* continuing from pretrained; with low coverage, consider domain-adaptive training or training from scratch
- [Separate two operations]{.hl}: giving released vectors to a downstream model as its initialization, and continuing the original embedding training. The second may require the output parameters and the training state, not only the `KeyedVectors`
:::

::: {.notes}
Domain shift and coverage matter alongside the amount of data. Examining the
neighbours of domain terms is a first check; the choice has to be confirmed on the
target task.
:::

## Intuition check 6 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
"Embeddings replaced TF-IDF." True or false?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- It depends on the task. On the single split here TF-IDF had the highest accuracy (0.853); its gap to averaged GloVe is hard to explain by chance in the paired test
- Lexical retrieval (BM25, for example) can be useful for exact term matching, dense retrieval for relations between different wordings
- Hybrid retrieval combines the two kinds of information; its performance has to be evaluated
- [Embedding vectors do not remove every use of TF-IDF or of one-hot encoding]{.hl}: selecting an embedding row can be written as a matrix product with a one-hot vector
:::

::: {.notes}
The gap to the doc2vec rows could not be measured: the predictions cannot be
reproduced exactly.
:::

## Interview-style questions for discussion

::: {.lede}
Three of the chapter's twelve questions: one on the objective, one on the geometry, one on system design.
:::

1. Explain word2vec to someone who knows regression but not neural networks.
2. Two unrelated words have cosine 0.3. Is that high or low?
3. You have 100,000 items and click logs. Design an item embedding.

::: {.src}
General preparation resources: Huyen 2021 and the *AIMLInterviews* repository
:::

::: {.notes}
On sourcing: these questions were written for working through the concepts and the
practical decisions of the chapter; no claim is made that they were asked at
particular companies. For general preparation, see Chip Huyen's Introduction to
Machine Learning Interviews and the AIMLInterviews repository on GitHub.

The chapter's other questions, as homework: skip-gram versus CBOW and when to
prefer each; why the 0.75 exponent; how subsampling can affect speed and the
quality of the representation; what to watch for in the king − man + woman demo;
why semantic search returns antonyms and what to do; document vectors for 50
million documents under 100 ms; embeddings trained on your own corpus coming out
worse than pretrained; detecting that a production embedding has gone stale; the
connection between PPMI+SVD, word2vec and GloVe.

Suggested format: pairs, one question per pair, two minutes; then the next slide.
:::

## What a strong answer names

::: {.compact}
1. **Skip-gram with negative sampling** — observed pairs positive, pairs from the noise sampler negative. The score is the dot product of two vectors, the probability $\sigma(v \cdot u)$, the derivative of one term $\sigma(v \cdot u) - y$. The form of the loss is shared with logistic regression; both tables are learned, so the problem is not convex. Then the $\mathrm{PMI} - \log K$ connection, with its conditions
2. **A reference distribution** — in the sample from the first 50,000 GloVe words the mean is 0.029 and the standard deviation 0.119; 0.3 is about 2.3 standard deviations up. High relative to the sample; no normal distribution, p-value or guaranteed semantic relation is implied. Look at the percentiles of your own data and at labelled pairs
3. **Skip-gram on sessions** — session = sequence of items. Airbnb: the booked listing as an additional positive context; within-market negatives *added to* the general ones (Grbovic & Cheng 2018). Session boundaries, the definition of a negative and the time split have to be explicit. Cold start: content features such as title and category
:::

::: {.notes}
The longer answers from the chapter.

1. The actual low-rank model and PPMI–SVD use different losses and different
   transformations of the target; they need not give the same result.
2. Centring removes the shared mean (Mu, Bhat and Viswanath 2018); it does not
   remove all anisotropy.
3. It should not be assumed that splitting arbitrary item IDs into character
   pieces carries meaning.
:::

## Exercises

:::: {.columns .compact}

::: {.column width="50%"}
1. **Compare the small example** for windows 1 and 4. Which neighbourhoods change? Report it if the expected tendency does not show
2. **Limits of analogies**: three that give the expected answer, three that do not; normalization and filter fixed; compare with the nearest-neighbour baseline
3. **Audit your own domain**: twenty terms; criterion fixed in advance; Spearman between grades and frequency rank
4. **Vocabulary coverage**: OOV learning curves in Turkish and English with fixed test sets
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
5. **The limit of averaging**: two sentences with the same tokens in a different order; which relation is lost?
6. **TF-IDF and dense representations**: choose settings on validation data, test only at the end; discuss it if there is no gain
7. **Implement CBOW yourself**: extend the NumPy example; same data and budget, compared by frequency group
8. **Explore an association direction**: fix pairs and terms in advance; compare the structure after removing the direction
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The chapter's eight exercises, abbreviated. Details worth reading out:

3. Grade the lists preferably without seeing the frequency rank; count
   out-of-vocabulary terms separately. A twenty-term result is exploratory.
4. Choose two corpora as similar as possible in topic, period and preprocessing.
   Do not derive an exact token requirement from type/token and hapax ratios alone.
6. Options: doc2vec settings, different dimensions, weighted representations such
   as SIF (Arora et al. 2017), or combinations.
7. Write down the difference you expect before the experiment. CS224N assignments
   change from year to year; if you use one, give the year and the direct link.
8. Do not produce the group labels by looking at the outcome of the operation.
   Present your small experiment as an exploration inspired by Gonen and
   Goldberg's study, not as a replication of it.

The expected observations are checkpoints, not an answer key: it is possible, for
example, that no candidate beats TF-IDF; the ordering of CBOW and skip-gram depends
on the data and the training budget.
:::

## Where to go deeper

| resource | why |
|:----------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| [Mikolov et al. 2013a](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781), [2013b](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546) | skip-gram and CBOW; then negative sampling and subsampling — read the second alongside the chapter's code |
| [Rong 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.2738) · [Goldberg & Levy 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.3722) | the gradients derived step by step; the reasoning behind the negative-sampling objective |
| [Levy & Goldberg 2014](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5477-neural-word-embedding-as-implicit-matrix-factorization) · [Levy et al. 2015](https://aclanthology.org/Q15-1016/) | the SGNS–PMI relation and the effect of hyperparameters |
| [Bolukbasi et al. 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06520), then [Gonen & Goldberg 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03862) | read together: the proposed operations, then an examination of what remains |
| [Jurafsky & Martin, Chapter 5](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/5.pdf) | word representations in the August 19, 2026 draft; Appendix J for PPMI; free |
| [Stanford CS224N](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/) | notes of the word-vectors lecture; the assignments change from year to year |
| [Elena Voita, NLP Course For You](https://lena-voita.github.io/nlp_course/word_embeddings.html) | skip-gram and negative sampling, with visuals |
| [fastText pretrained vectors](https://fasttext.cc/docs/en/crawl-vectors.html) | released vectors for 157 languages including Turkish |

::: {.notes}
From the chapter's list.

Papers, in reading order, all free: Mikolov et al., "Efficient Estimation of Word
Representations in Vector Space" and then "Distributed Representations of Words and
Phrases"; Xin Rong, "word2vec Parameter Learning Explained" — derives the gradients
of CBOW, skip-gram and the related output objectives step by step — together with
Goldberg and Levy's "word2vec Explained"; Levy and Goldberg, "Neural Word Embedding
as Implicit Matrix Factorization", and Levy, Goldberg and Dagan, "Improving
Distributional Similarity with Lessons Learned"; GloVe (Pennington et al. 2014) and
"Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information" (Bojanowski et al. 2017);
Bolukbasi et al. and then "Lipstick on a Pig".

CS224N: on the Winter 2026 page the first assignment is an introduction to word
vectors and the second covers neural network foundations, tensor derivatives and
dependency parsing.

To watch: CS224N Lecture 1, word2vec derived at the board; Google's "Visualizing
High-Dimensional Space" video.

Hands on: gensim and its word2vec tutorial; Jay Alammar's "The Illustrated
Word2vec" (visual explanations) and Sebastian Ruder's "On Word Embeddings"
(historical and methodological development); TensorFlow Projector — look up your

:::
